To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the NP gene of CCHF virus is highly diverse, with the highest diversity in a virus isolated from a tick collected in Greece, and (ii) recombinant NP antigens derived from two genetically diverse strains, one from a human infection and one from a tick, reacted with antibodies of 13/14 patients who survived infection with CCHFV, indicating that these recombinant antigents have application as a diagnostic tool and in serosurveillance.
we have determined the genetic diversity of CCHF viruses and developed an ELISA to detect antibodies against CCHF viruses.
we developed a safe, recombinant nucleocapsid-based ELISA that can be used to detect IgG antibodies against CCHF in patients from South Africa, a region that has a high burden of CCHF.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic diversity of CCHF virus, the preparation of recombinant nucleocapsid antigens and the development of a diagnostic ELISA for the detection of CCHF antibodies in human sera.
the development of a safe, cost-effective and reliable diagnostic tool for the detection of IgG antibody in patients infected with CCHFV.
the development of a safe and cost-effective diagnostic test for CCHFV and the use of recombinant CCHFV antigens for the development of vaccines.

The main takeaway from our work is that
recombinant CCHFV NP can be prepared using codon-optimized gene fragments from different CCHFV genotypes.
the recombinant nucleocapsid protein (NP) of CCHF virus is highly conserved, and the NP can be used as a universal antigen for serological diagnosis of CCHF.
recombinant NP antigens prepared from genetically diverse CCHV strains can be used for the detection of IgG antibodies in patients who survived CCHFV infection.
